questions.stem: The 'MASTER GLAND' of the endocrine system is the:
questions.explanation: PITUITARY GLAND (hypophysis) — 'MASTER GLAND' of the endocrine system. LOCATION: at base of brain, in SELLA TURCICA (saddle-shaped depression of sphenoid bone); connected to hypothalamus by INFUNDIBULUM (pituitary stalk). SIZE: pea-sized (~0.5g). 2 ANATOMICAL LOBES with different origins + functions: (1) ANTERIOR PITUITARY (ADENOHYPOPHYSIS) — derived from oral ectoderm (Rathke's pouch); secretes 6 MAJOR HORMONES: (a) GROWTH HORMONE (GH / Somatotropin) — growth of bones + tissues; excess = gigantism (children) / acromegaly (adults); deficiency = dwarfism. (b) PROLACTIN — MILK production in lactation. (c) TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone) — stimulates thyroid to produce T3, T4. (d) ACTH (AdrenoCorticoTropic Hormone) — stimulates adrenal cortex to produce cortisol. (e) FSH (Follicle Stimulating Hormone) — ovarian follicle development / spermatogenesis. (f) LH (Luteinizing Hormone) — ovulation + corpus luteum / testosterone production. (2) POSTERIOR PITUITARY (NEUROHYPOPHYSIS) — neural origin; STORES + RELEASES (doesn't synthesise) 2 hormones made in hypothalamus: (a) ADH (AntiDiuretic Hormone / Vasopressin) — water retention by kidneys; deficiency = Diabetes Insipidus (excess dilute urine). (b) OXYTOCIN — uterine contraction during labor; milk let-down in lactation; 'love hormone' — bonding, trust, social behaviour. HYPOTHALAMUS — controls pituitary via: (a) RELEASING hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH) + INHIBITING hormones (somatostatin, dopamine as PIH) delivered via hypophyseal portal blood vessels to anterior pituitary; (b) AXONAL transport for posterior pituitary hormones. CLINICAL: (1) TUMORS (adenomas, microadenoma or macroadenoma) — 80% of pituitary tumors; can secrete excess GH, ACTH, prolactin. (2) SHEEHAN'S SYNDROME — postpartum hemorrhage causes pituitary necrosis → hypopituitarism. (3) PANHYPOPITUITARISM. OTHER major ENDOCRINE glands: Thyroid (T3, T4, calcitonin), Parathyroid (PTH — calcium), Adrenal (cortisol, aldosterone, epinephrine), Pancreas (insulin, glucagon), Ovaries (estrogen, progesterone), Testes (testosterone), Pineal (melatonin — sleep), Thymus (thymosin). Also 'DIFFUSE' endocrine: stomach (ghrelin), kidney (EPO + renin + 1-hydroxylase), liver (IGF-1), fat (leptin, adiponectin), heart (ANP, BNP). pea-sized, at base of brain; controlled by HYPOTHALAMUS; regulates thyroid, adrenals, gonads, growth, milk, water.

questions.stem: INSULIN, secreted by the PANCREAS, is produced by which cells?

options.option_text: BETA CELLS of Islets of Langerhans

questions.explanation: PANCREAS — DUAL-function (ENDOCRINE + EXOCRINE) organ in the abdomen behind stomach. EXOCRINE (95% of pancreas mass): ACINAR CELLS secrete digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen) into pancreatic duct → duodenum. ENDOCRINE (~2%): clustered in ~1 MILLION 'ISLETS OF LANGERHANS' (discovered 1869 by Paul Langerhans, German pathologist). 5 CELL TYPES in islets: (1) ALPHA (α) cells (~20%) — secrete GLUCAGON — RAISES blood glucose (stimulates glycogenolysis + gluconeogenesis in liver). Released when blood sugar LOW. (2) BETA (β) cells (~70%) — secrete INSULIN — LOWERS blood glucose. Also amylin. Released when blood sugar HIGH. (3) DELTA (δ) cells (~5%) — secrete SOMATOSTATIN — INHIBITS both insulin + glucagon secretion; also paracrine. (4) PP cells (F cells) — secrete pancreatic polypeptide; regulates pancreatic function + appetite. (5) EPSILON cells — secrete GHRELIN. INSULIN: discovered 1921-22 by BANTING + BEST (Toronto) with Macleod + Collip. Nobel 1923. First treated DIABETIC: LEONARD THOMPSON (14 yr, Jan 1922). 51-amino-acid peptide; made as preproinsulin → proinsulin → INSULIN + C-peptide. STRUCTURE: 2 chains (A = 21 aa, B = 30 aa) linked by disulfide bonds. FUNCTIONS: (a) facilitates glucose uptake into muscle + adipose (via GLUT4 translocation); (b) promotes glycogenesis in liver + muscle; (c) lipogenesis (fat storage); (d) protein synthesis; (e) inhibits gluconeogenesis + glycogenolysis. DIABETES MELLITUS: (1) TYPE 1 — autoimmune destruction of β cells → absolute insulin deficiency; children + young; needs insulin therapy. (2) TYPE 2 — insulin RESISTANCE + relative deficiency; adults; obesity-linked; managed with diet + exercise + oral hypoglycaemics (metformin, sulphonylureas, DPP-4i, SGLT2i) + insulin when needed. (3) GESTATIONAL DM — during pregnancy. (4) MODY — monogenic young-adult type. 77 million Indians have diabetes (ICMR-INDIAB study 2023) — 'Diabetic capital of world' with China. Also 136 million pre-diabetic. HbA1c target <7% for most diabetics. COMPLICATIONS: retinopathy (diabetic eye), nephropathy, neuropathy, foot ulcers, CVD, stroke. World Diabetes Day = 14 NOVEMBER (Banting's birthday). make INSULIN, lowering blood glucose by promoting cellular uptake + glycogenesis.

questions.stem: The THYROID hormones T3 (Triiodothyronine) + T4 (Thyroxine) contain the element:
questions.explanation: THYROID GLAND — BUTTERFLY-shaped gland in NECK (front, below Adam's apple). 2 LOBES connected by isthmus. Produces: (1) T4 (Thyroxine) — 90% of thyroid output; 4 iodines on tyrosine backbone. (2) T3 (Triiodothyronine) — 10% of thyroid output but MORE ACTIVE (3-4× T4). 80% of circulating T3 is made by peripheral conversion of T4 by DEIODINASES (liver, kidney). (3) CALCITONIN — by parafollicular C cells; lowers blood calcium (opposite of PTH). SYNTHESIS: follicular cells concentrate IODIDE via Na/I symporter; oxidise I- to I+ via thyroid peroxidase (TPO); iodinate tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin → MIT + DIT → couple to form T3 + T4 within thyroglobulin; stored in COLLOID; upon stimulation, TG endocytosed + hydrolysed to release T3 + T4 into blood. FUNCTIONS of T3/T4: (1) BASAL METABOLIC RATE — increases; (2) increases cardiac output + heart rate; (3) brain development (crucial in fetal + infantile life — deficiency = cretinism); (4) bone growth + maturation; (5) digestive motility; (6) muscle function; (7) reproduction. REGULATION: hypothalamus-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) AXIS: HYPOTHALAMUS (TRH) → PITUITARY (TSH) → THYROID (T3, T4) → negative feedback on TSH + TRH. DISORDERS: (1) HYPOTHYROIDISM — ↓ T3/T4, ↑TSH. Symptoms: fatigue, cold intolerance, weight GAIN, dry skin, hair loss, constipation, bradycardia, depression, goiter (if iodine deficit). CAUSES: Hashimoto's thyroiditis (autoimmune, most common in developed world), iodine deficiency (developing world — now reduced by iodised salt), drug-induced, post-surgical / radioablation. Treatment: LEVOTHYROXINE (synthetic T4, daily). CRETINISM — congenital hypothyroidism — stunted growth + mental retardation; preventable by newborn TSH screening + early thyroxine. (2) HYPERTHYROIDISM — ↑ T3/T4, ↓TSH. Symptoms: heat intolerance, weight LOSS despite good appetite, tremor, palpitations, anxiety, diarrhea, exophthalmos (Graves'). Causes: GRAVES' DISEASE (autoimmune TSH receptor antibodies, commonest; exophthalmos + pretibial myxedema); toxic multinodular goiter; subacute thyroiditis. Treatment: anti-thyroid drugs (carbimazole, methimazole, PTU), radioiodine (I-131), thyroidectomy. (3) GOITER — enlarged thyroid; iodine-deficient (endemic) or due to Hashimoto / Graves / nodules. (4) THYROID CANCER — papillary (most common + best prognosis), follicular, medullary (parafollicular C cells), anaplastic (aggressive). 3 atoms in T3, 4 in T4; iodine deficiency causes GOITRE + cretinism in children; thyroid hormones regulate METABOLISM.

questions.stem: The 'FIGHT OR FLIGHT' hormone, secreted by the ADRENAL MEDULLA during stress, is:
questions.explanation: ADRENAL GLANDS — pair of pyramid-shaped glands on top of each KIDNEY (hence 'suprarenal'). TWO DISTINCT REGIONS with different origins + hormones: (1) ADRENAL CORTEX (outer 80%) — mesodermal origin; 3 zones secreting STEROID hormones (ALL made from cholesterol): (a) ZONA GLOMERULOSA (outermost) — MINERALOCORTICOIDS, chiefly ALDOSTERONE — regulates Na retention + K excretion by kidney tubules; BP control. Controlled by RAAS (Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System). Excess = Conn's syndrome (hyperaldosteronism). (b) ZONA FASCICULATA (middle) — GLUCOCORTICOIDS, chiefly CORTISOL — 'stress hormone'; mobilises glucose (gluconeogenesis) + fat + protein breakdown; ANTI-INFLAMMATORY + IMMUNOSUPPRESSIVE; diurnal rhythm (peak morning). Excess = Cushing's syndrome (moon face, truncal obesity, buffalo hump, purple striae, hypertension, diabetes). Controlled by ACTH from pituitary. (c) ZONA RETICULARIS (innermost) — ADRENAL ANDROGENS (DHEA, androstenedione) — sex hormone precursors; small in males (testes dominate), meaningful in females. (2) ADRENAL MEDULLA (inner 20%) — neural crest origin (modified sympathetic ganglia); CHROMAFFIN cells produce catecholamines: ADRENALINE / EPINEPHRINE (~80%) + NORADRENALINE (~20%) + dopamine. STRESS response — 'FIGHT or FLIGHT': triggered by SYMPATHETIC nervous system → adrenal medulla releases catecholamines → (a) increased HEART RATE + contractility; (b) increased BP; (c) BRONCHODILATION; (d) PUPIL DILATION; (e) GLYCOGENOLYSIS in liver + muscle → raised blood glucose; (f) LIPOLYSIS — fat mobilisation; (g) vasoconstriction in skin + viscera, vasodilation in muscle; (h) sweating; (i) anxiety + alertness. ADRENALINE is the DRUG OF CHOICE in: (1) ANAPHYLAXIS (EpiPen 0.3 mg IM); (2) CARDIAC ARREST (CPR protocol, 1 mg IV); (3) Severe asthma; (4) Local anaesthesia (mixed with lidocaine for vasoconstriction + prolonged effect). PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA — catecholamine-secreting adrenal medulla tumor; causes episodic hypertension + headache + palpitations + sweating ('5 H's'); rare. ADDISON's DISEASE (Thomas Addison, 1855) — adrenal cortex hypofunction (all 3 zones); tiredness, weight loss, hyperpigmentation, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia; treated with glucocorticoid + mineralocorticoid replacement. CUSHING's DISEASE — pituitary cause of Cushing's syndrome; other causes exogenous steroids, adrenal tumor, ectopic ACTH (lung cancer). NOTABLE: J.F. Kennedy had undiagnosed Addison's for years. rapid-action catecholamine; raises HR, BP, blood sugar; dilates pupils + bronchi.

questions.stem: The PRIMARY FEMALE SEX HORMONES are:
questions.explanation: FEMALE SEX HORMONES — primarily produced by OVARIES (also small amounts from adrenals, fat). (1) ESTROGEN (3 types): (a) ESTRADIOL (E2) — most potent + most abundant in reproductive years; (b) ESTRIOL (E3) — predominant in pregnancy (produced by placenta); (c) ESTRONE (E1) — dominant post-menopause. FUNCTIONS: (1) Development of SECONDARY SEXUAL CHARACTERISTICS at puberty — breast, wider hips, fat distribution, pubic hair, menarche. (2) Regulates MENSTRUAL CYCLE — follicular phase dominance; triggers LH surge leading to ovulation. (3) UTERINE lining (endometrium) proliferation. (4) Bone density maintenance — estrogen loss post-menopause → osteoporosis risk. (5) Cardiovascular protection in pre-menopause. (6) Mood, skin elasticity, metabolism, memory. (2) PROGESTERONE — produced mainly by CORPUS LUTEUM after ovulation + by placenta in pregnancy. FUNCTIONS: (a) Prepares + maintains UTERINE LINING for embryo implantation; 'pro-gestation' hormone. (b) Prevents contraction of uterus during pregnancy (hence 'progesterone' = 'favouring gestation'). (c) Breast gland development. (d) Inhibits ovulation (basis of oral contraceptives). (e) thermogenic effect (BBT rises after ovulation). MENSTRUAL CYCLE (28 days typical): (a) FOLLICULAR PHASE (day 1-13): FSH stimulates follicle growth; estrogen rises. (b) OVULATION (day 14): LH SURGE triggers ovulation. (c) LUTEAL PHASE (day 15-28): corpus luteum makes progesterone + estrogen; if no pregnancy, CL degenerates → progesterone drops → menstruation starts (day 1). Cycle resets. MENARCHE (first period) ~10-13 years; MENOPAUSE (last period) ~45-55 years. CONTRACEPTION: combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) = estrogen + progestin; progestin-only pills; IUDs (hormonal or copper); patches, rings, injectables, implants (Nexplanon, DMPA), emergency (Plan B = levonorgestrel). MALE SEX HORMONES — primarily TESTOSTERONE (produced by Leydig cells of testes under LH; also small amounts from adrenals; in women ovaries + adrenals make small amount). FUNCTIONS: (a) spermatogenesis (with FSH); (b) secondary sexual characters at puberty — deepening voice, facial + body hair, muscle mass, Adam's apple; (c) libido; (d) bone + muscle mass; (e) anabolic. DHT (dihydrotestosterone) — from testosterone via 5-alpha reductase; responsible for external genital development in fetus, male-pattern baldness, prostate enlargement. HRT (Hormone Replacement Therapy) in menopause is controversial — short-term for symptoms, not long-term due to breast cancer + clot risk (Women's Health Initiative 2002). produced by ovaries; estrogen for secondary sexual characters, progesterone for pregnancy.

questions.stem: MELATONIN, which regulates the sleep-wake cycle, is secreted by the:
questions.explanation: PINEAL GLAND (epiphysis cerebri) — small PEA-SIZED endocrine gland deep in center of brain (between the two hemispheres, in grooves of thalamus). Size ~5-8 mm, weight ~150 mg. Described by Galen (~2nd c. CE); Descartes famously called it the 'seat of the soul' + 'principal seat of the soul' (17th c.). FUNCTION: produces MELATONIN (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) — hormone that regulates the CIRCADIAN (daily) SLEEP-WAKE cycle. MECHANISM: (1) LIGHT signals from RETINA reach SCN (SUPRACHIASMATIC NUCLEUS) of hypothalamus — the 'master clock'. (2) SCN signals via multisynaptic pathway to pineal gland. (3) In DARKNESS — pineal INCREASES melatonin production (rises sharply after sunset, peaks 2-4 AM, falls before wake). (4) In LIGHT — pineal melatonin production is SUPPRESSED. (5) Blue light from screens = potent suppressor → why phone + TV before bed disrupts sleep. USES of melatonin: (a) JET LAG mitigation; (b) shift-work sleep disorder; (c) insomnia (mild benefit, particularly sleep-onset insomnia); (d) non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder in blind individuals. Available as OTC supplement in many countries (doses 0.3-10 mg). CIRCADIAN RHYTHM discovery: J.C. HALL, M. ROSBASH, M.W. YOUNG got Nobel Physiology 2017 for molecular mechanisms of circadian clock. FLIES + humans share 'period' + 'timeless' clock genes. CIRCADIAN DISRUPTION linked to: insomnia, depression, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, cancer (WHO classified shift-work as possibly carcinogenic 2007). Shift workers, pilots, travellers particularly affected. OTHER pineal products: SEROTONIN precursor for melatonin; 5-HIAA; glucosamine. PINEAL CALCIFIES with age (visible on X-ray/CT — 'pineal calcification' useful landmark in neurology). SEASONAL AFFECTIVE DISORDER (SAD) — depression in winter months due to reduced daylight → melatonin + serotonin changes; treated with LIGHT THERAPY (bright light box mornings, 10,000 lux, 30 min). OTHER MINOR endocrine sites: (1) HEART (right atrium) — ANP + BNP (vasodilators, natriuretic). (2) STOMACH — ghrelin (hunger). (3) ADIPOSE — LEPTIN (satiety), adiponectin. (4) KIDNEYS — EPO (RBC production), RENIN, calcitriol (active Vit D). (5) LIVER — IGF-1, thrombopoietin, angiotensinogen. (6) INTESTINES — numerous (GLP-1, CCK, PYY, secretin, gastrin). (7) PLACENTA — hCG, hPL, estrogen, progesterone. (8) SKIN — Vit D synthesis, cytokines. pea-sized, deep in brain; activity inversely linked to light; melatonin released in darkness promoting sleep.

questions.stem: PARATHYROID hormone (PTH) regulates BLOOD CALCIUM levels by:
questions.explanation: PARATHYROID GLANDS — 4 small pea-sized glands on POSTERIOR surface of THYROID gland (NOT same as thyroid). Secrete PARATHYROID HORMONE (PTH, parathormone) — main regulator of CALCIUM + PHOSPHATE homeostasis. NORMAL BLOOD CALCIUM 8.5-10.5 mg/dL. PTH RELEASED WHEN Ca++ LOW → 3 ACTIONS to RAISE Ca: (1) BONES — stimulates OSTEOCLASTS (via RANK-RANKL) → bone resorption → releases Ca + Pi into blood. (2) KIDNEYS — (a) INCREASES Ca reabsorption in distal convoluted tubule; (b) INHIBITS phosphate reabsorption → more phosphate lost in urine (phosphaturic effect); (c) ACTIVATES 1-α-hydroxylase converting 25-OH-Vit D to ACTIVE CALCITRIOL (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D). (3) INTESTINES (indirectly via calcitriol) — INCREASES Ca + Pi absorption from diet. OVERALL: Ca UP, phosphate DOWN. OPPOSING HORMONE: CALCITONIN — produced by PARAFOLLICULAR C CELLS of thyroid; LOWERS blood calcium (inhibits osteoclasts + increases kidney Ca excretion); minor role in humans but salmon calcitonin used in medicine. VITAMIN D — fat-soluble vitamin + hormone: (a) Synthesised in SKIN from 7-dehydrocholesterol on UV-B exposure → cholecalciferol (D3); (b) Hydroxylated in liver to 25-OH-D (calcidiol, storage form, measured clinically); (c) Hydroxylated in kidney to 1,25-(OH)2-D (CALCITRIOL, active form). ACTIONS: (1) Ca + Pi absorption in gut; (2) bone mineralisation; (3) calcium mobilisation from bone with PTH; (4) immune modulation; (5) cell differentiation. VIT D DEFICIENCY: Rickets (children — bowed legs, delayed teeth, poor growth), Osteomalacia (adults — soft bones, pain). Very common in India — 70-80% of population estimated deficient/insufficient despite sunshine (due to clothing, vegetarian diet, indoor lifestyles, dark skin, fat absorption). Fortification of milk + edible oils + weekly 60,000 IU supplementation. DISORDERS of CALCIUM regulation: (1) HYPERPARATHYROIDISM — excess PTH (usually parathyroid adenoma); high Ca, low Pi; osteoporosis, kidney stones, 'stones, bones, abdominal groans, psychic moans'. (2) HYPOPARATHYROIDISM — low PTH (post-thyroid surgery accident, DiGeorge); low Ca → tetany (muscle spasms, Chvostek + Trousseau signs), seizures. (3) Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PTH receptor resistance). (4) HYPERCALCEMIA causes: malignancy (10%), HyperPTH (90%), granulomatous diseases, Milk-alkali. Rule 'CHIMPANZEES' mnemonic. (a) bone resorption (osteoclasts); (b) kidney calcium reabsorption; (c) activates Vit D → ↑ gut Ca absorption.

questions.stem: The hormone OXYTOCIN, often called the 'LOVE HORMONE' or 'BONDING HORMONE', is released from the:
questions.explanation: OXYTOCIN — 9-amino acid peptide; produced in PARAVENTRICULAR + SUPRAOPTIC NUCLEI of HYPOTHALAMUS; stored + released from POSTERIOR PITUITARY. PHYSIOLOGICAL ROLES: (1) CHILDBIRTH (parturition) — Positive feedback loop: cervix stretching → oxytocin release → uterine contractions → more stretching → more oxytocin → labor progression; synthetic version (PITOCIN) used medically to induce or augment labor. (2) MILK EJECTION / LET-DOWN reflex — infant suckling → nipple stimulation → hypothalamus → oxytocin → myoepithelial cells around alveoli contract → milk flows out into ducts. (3) PAIR BONDING + MATERNAL INSTINCT + SOCIAL BEHAVIOUR — nicknamed 'LOVE HORMONE', 'cuddle hormone', 'bonding hormone'. Released during hugging, kissing, orgasm, breast-feeding, skin-skin contact (e.g., 'kangaroo care' of newborn). (4) TRUST + social cognition — intranasal oxytocin studies show increased trust + empathy (Kosfeld et al. 2005). (5) Orgasm — released during sexual climax in both sexes; contributes to pair-bonding post-coital. CLINICAL uses of OXYTOCIN: (1) INDUCTION of LABOR (Pitocin IV drip); (2) AUGMENTATION of weak labor contractions; (3) PREVENTION + TREATMENT of POSTPARTUM HEMORRHAGE (uterine atony) — oxytocin contracts uterus to seal blood vessels; world's most commonly used life-saving drug in obstetrics. (4) Milk let-down failure. PROPOSED (experimental) uses: autism (improving social cognition), PTSD, depression. ADH / VASOPRESSIN — other posterior pituitary hormone: (1) WATER retention — acts on V2 receptors of kidney collecting ducts → aquaporin insertion → water reabsorption. (2) VASOCONSTRICTION via V1a receptors → BP rise. DEFICIENCY = DIABETES INSIPIDUS — excessive dilute urine (>3L/day), severe thirst. 2 TYPES: (a) central DI (pituitary doesn't make ADH — head injury, tumor); (b) nephrogenic DI (kidney doesn't respond — lithium, hypercalcemia). Treat central DI with DDAVP (desmopressin, synthetic ADH analog; also used for nocturnal enuresis in kids + von Willebrand disease / mild hemophilia A). EXCESS ADH = SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH) — water retention, hyponatremia, confusion; causes: small cell lung cancer, CNS infections, drugs. PREDICTIVE connection: oxytocin + ADH differ in 2 amino acids only; both 9-peptide; both cyclic (disulfide bond) — evolved from common ancestral hormone (vasotocin in lower vertebrates). roles in childbirth, lactation, orgasm, social bonding + trust; stored there; produced in hypothalamus.

questions.stem: GROWTH HORMONE (GH) excess during CHILDHOOD (before closure of growth plates) leads to:
questions.explanation: GROWTH HORMONE (GH / Somatotropin) — 191-amino acid peptide from SOMATOTROPHS of ANTERIOR PITUITARY. Pulsatile secretion, MAX during DEEP SLEEP + after exercise + fasting. EFFECTS: (1) DIRECT — lipolysis (fat breakdown), protein synthesis, gluconeogenesis (raises blood glucose — 'anti-insulin'), Na retention. (2) INDIRECT (via IGF-1, 'insulin-like growth factor 1' made in LIVER in response to GH) — LONGITUDINAL BONE GROWTH (via epiphyseal chondrocyte proliferation), organ growth, muscle growth, cell proliferation. REGULATION: hypothalamus controls via GHRH (Growth Hormone Releasing Hormone, stimulatory) + SOMATOSTATIN / GHIH (inhibitory). Also ghrelin (stomach) stimulates; IGF-1 negative feedback. DISORDERS of GH: (1) DEFICIENCY IN CHILDREN — DWARFISM ('GH-deficient dwarfism', pituitary dwarfism) — normal proportions, short stature. Differs from achondroplasia (autosomal dominant, bone disorder, not GH). Treated with recombinant GH injections (Somatropin) until growth plates close. (2) DEFICIENCY IN ADULTS — GHD in adults; fatigue, central obesity, reduced muscle + bone, mood changes. Treated if severe. (3) EXCESS BEFORE EPIPHYSEAL CLOSURE (children) — GIGANTISM. Over-growth of long bones → extreme height. Famous cases: Robert Wadlow (8 ft 11.1 in, 1918-40, tallest man in recorded history) + Sandy Allen (7 ft 7) + Sultan Kösen (8 ft 3, current tallest living). Often due to pituitary adenoma. (4) EXCESS AFTER EPIPHYSEAL CLOSURE (adults) — ACROMEGALY. Since bones can't grow in length, they grow in WIDTH + soft tissues enlarge. Features: enlarged hands, feet (shoe size increases), jaw (prognathism), nose, tongue, frontal bossing, organomegaly (cardiomegaly, hepatomegaly), skin thickening, sweating, joint pains, diabetes. Diagnosis: IGF-1 + OGTT (failure to suppress GH); pituitary MRI. Treatment: transsphenoidal surgery for pituitary adenoma; medications (somatostatin analogs — octreotide, lanreotide; GH receptor antagonist — pegvisomant); radiotherapy. ABUSE of GH: atthletes + bodybuilders illicitly use GH + IGF-1 + anabolic steroids — banned by WADA; risks: acromegaly-like features, cancer risk, joint damage, diabetes. SHORT STATURE in India — commonly due to undernutrition, endocrine (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency), chronic diseases (celiac, IBD), genetic (Turner syndrome in girls). MID-DAY MEAL + PM POSHAN address nutritional component. abnormally tall stature (often 7-8+ ft); vs ACROMEGALY (adults) with enlarged extremities, face, organs.

questions.stem: Which hormone TRIGGERS OVULATION in the menstrual cycle?
questions.explanation: OVULATION — release of mature ovum from ovarian follicle — triggered by LH SURGE (Luteinizing Hormone surge). MENSTRUAL CYCLE in detail (28 days typical; 21-35 normal): (1) FOLLICULAR PHASE (day 1-13): (a) menstruation starts day 1 (shedding of endometrium when previous cycle's corpus luteum regresses + progesterone falls); (b) FSH rises → recruits ~10-20 primary follicles → one DOMINANT FOLLICLE; (c) granulosa cells of follicle produce ESTROGEN (via aromatisation of androgens); (d) estrogen rises through follicular phase; (e) INITIALLY estrogen has NEGATIVE FEEDBACK on LH/FSH; but when estrogen crosses a threshold (~200 pg/ml for 48 hrs), it flips to POSITIVE FEEDBACK on LH → LH SURGE. (2) OVULATION (day 14, ~24-36 HRS AFTER LH surge start): LH surge causes (a) rupture of follicle; (b) release of OOCYTE into peritoneal cavity; (c) oocyte picked up by fimbriae + enters FALLOPIAN TUBE. FERTILISATION, if it occurs, happens in AMPULLA of fallopian tube within 24 HOURS of ovulation. (3) LUTEAL PHASE (day 15-28): (a) Ruptured follicle becomes CORPUS LUTEUM (yellow body) — produces PROGESTERONE + estrogen. (b) Endometrium becomes 'SECRETORY' — glycogen-rich + vascular, prepared for embryo. (c) IF no pregnancy — CL degenerates after ~14 days (luteolysis) → progesterone + estrogen fall → endometrium shed = menstruation → new cycle. (d) IF PREGNANCY — implanting embryo's trophoblast makes hCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin) → RESCUES the corpus luteum → progesterone maintained for 10-12 weeks of pregnancy; placenta takes over by 12 weeks. hCG = basis of pregnancy tests (urine or blood). OVULATION PREDICTOR KITS (OPKs) detect LH surge in urine to time intercourse. BBT (basal body temperature) rises ~0.3-0.6°C after ovulation (progesterone's thermogenic effect) — retrospective indicator. Cervical mucus changes (clear, stretchy, 'egg white' at ovulation — maximum fertility). MITTELSCHMERZ — mid-cycle pain, ovulation pain on one side. OVARIAN RESERVE — fixed at birth (~2 million primordial follicles), declines to ~400K at menarche, <1000 at menopause. Only ~400 ovulate in lifetime. AMH (Anti-Mullerian Hormone) blood test = measure of ovarian reserve. Fertility declines after 35; MENOPAUSE average age 51 years. ~24-36 hrs before ovulation; ovulation tests detect LH; typically around Day 13-14 of 28-day cycle; Luteinizing Hormone.
